newsitem.title: USA: WALL ST WEEK AHEAD/Critical data after downdraft.
newsitem.headline: WALL ST WEEK AHEAD/Critical data after downdraft.

text.p: Two pieces of critical economic data will be the focus on Wall Street this week following Thursday's steep stock downturn.
On Tuesday the National Association of Purchasing Management's March survey is reported, followed by March employment data on Friday.
If the data show the U.S. economy remains robust, it would further convince Wall Street that more Federal Reserve interest rate hikes are in the works.
That, in turn, would push bond yields higher, making bonds more attractive than stocks and spark a flight of money out of equities, market analysts said.
"There's no doubt many investors have begun to shift from stocks to bonds, and I don't believe this shift is over," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 140 points on Thursday, ending at 6740.59. The blue-chip gauge recovered at the close after falling as many as 217 points.
It ended the week with a 64-point loss.

Last Tuesday, the Federal Reserve raised the federal funds rate by a quarter percentage point to 5.50 percent. Strong economic data triggered a sharp selloff in bonds Thursday, the last trading session before the three-day Easter weekend, with the long bond closing down 1-9/32 to yield 7.09 percent.
The seven-percent level in the long bond is viewed as a level at which investors start shifting assets to bonds and out of stocks.
Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer & Co, said the rise in rates domestically was part of a worldwide phenomenon.

"I think we are beginning to see a whole new monetary environment," he said. "Tactical asset allocators are much more likely to focus on the bond market with the yield above seven percent than on stocks with the Dow at 6,800. This is going to be a problem for the stock market."
Roy Blumberg, chief investment strategist at Josephthal Lyon & Ross, said that investors were worried about the effect that higher rates and a stronger dollar will have on corporate earnings.

"People are worried that the strong dollar and higher interest rates will take a bite out of earnings," Blumberg said. "Higher rates could cause a contraction in multiples so that earnings become the only thing that can move stocks."
